CVD seems to be a fairly accurate translation of QED. The Latin is "what was supposed to be shown"¹ and it looks like the Italian means something like "as it was desired to show"? The Italian isn't a relative clause, but the meaning looks basically the same.

children.text: To borrow the usual quote about ingenious fools, the trouble with "easily" disproving that False is in your context is that there are such ingenious proofs of False.  One can appear to be doing very substantial and sophisticated mathematics, encountering many obstacles along the way that look identical to what you'd face if you were relying on something true, only to realize much later that one of your hypotheses is uninhabited.  The concern was that were the Riemann Hypothesis false, a very, very large subset of modern mathematics might fall into this category.
But that's 100% wrong. If it was easy to prove surprising theorems from an assumption of the Riemann hypothesis, it would also be easy to disprove the Riemann hypothesis.

The value it adds is that those theorems are now actually true, which means all those derived results are "real" mathematics... as every mathematician knows, it is quite easy to prove very surprising theorems when False is in your context.

children.text:
> It wasn't assumed it was true

Are you claiming that there wasn't a significant majority of mathematicians who believed it true? That's all I'm saying. I can only assume we agree.

To expand on what I said though, if it is proven that P != NP then nothing really changes as that assumption is in line with everything we understand about computational complexity theory. The proof would really just suggest there's probably nothing that surprising to be found that we don't know.

If P = NP however that is far more likely to suggest we're missing something fundamental which could radical consequences for more practical fields like comp-sci. Similar can be said of GRH. Everything we know points in the direction of GRH being true, and while it may be interesting to prove these things, its much less likely to lead to some surprising and impactful downstream discoveries.

It wasn't assumed it was true. People thought a world in which it was true was more beautiful than one where it wasn't, but proving it true wasn't a pesky little detail.

In fact, there was a whole literature of papers proving that if the GRH was false in one particular way (the existence of Landau-Siegel zeroes) many theorems followed from it. For example, if there's a Landau-Siegal zero, the twin primes conjecture is true.

If value here is a measure of utility, its not super useful on its own that something that was almost universally assumed to be true is now known to be true.

But with a problem as difficult and fundamental as the Riemann Hypothesis the thought has always been that in the process of solving it we'd be likely to develop or discover something that did have real world utility. At least this is often what happened in the past, the obvious example here being Newton developing calculus, a field of mathematics which can be applied to other problems beyond the narrow set of problems he was trying to solve.

What I find interesting about this, if the claim holds up, is whether this will assumption will remain true, or if the value of these AI proofs is going to significantly lower than those of human discoveries in the past.

Maybe a good analogy here is to think about how all of tools we humans have created has been ultimately in the pursuit of solving some problem. For the developers here, consider this – if ChatGPT had existed before React, would React ever have been developed? I mean, if an LLM can brute force the same result with just vanilla JS the need to develop frameworks and libraries to solve what was once difficult for a human to solve drops.

I'll note that I'm playing devils advocate here as I think AIs would probably build something better than React had it not existed, but it's something to think about at least. I suspect there's a higher probability than some here are assigning that this proof ultimately ends up have relatively little utility.
Doesn't that increase the value?  We now know all of those results are true, where before we didn't.

In broader context the “being nice” part seems like both of them talking past each other.

What happened was the two researchers, Buckmaster and Alpoge (from TFA) solved a significant subset of Navier Stokes (referenced as “Euler”) which set off rumors.

Through whatever game of Chinese Whispers ensued, OpenAI thought they had solved the full Navier Stokes problem, which they hadn’t. So OpenAI pointed their latest unreleased model at it, and it actually solved the full problem!!

Pure George Danzig vibes on that one.

So when this meeting happened, the OpenAI folks were surprised that these researchers had NOT solved the full problem, only the subset. Yet from their perspective, they were offering them credit for the full problem, and so “we’re being nice.” The Anthropic employee (Alpoge) was clearly an optics issue and so they felt they didn’t have to be that nice.

But the other researcher, Buckmaster, was suspicious that their work had been stolen, and so was understandably in a combative mood. You can see that from his perspective they were not being “nice”, they were trying to scoop them, possibly on stolen work, and then bribe them with shared credit.

But they had not solved the full problem, and academic plagiarism is a very serious allegation that can ruin careers of both the accused and the accuser. So from OpenAI’s perspective it was like, why would you accuse us of plagiarism when you yourself have not solved the full problem and when we’re willing to share undue credit for it??

This was made worse by the fact that OpenAI would not categorically deny if the others’ work had been used for training until much much later. This was terrible optics, but anyone who’s dealt with large scale data pipelines compounded by privacy issues knows that it gets very difficult to trace these things, so it takes time to make a definitive statement.

Alpoge somehow seemed less troubled by this whole episode, but I guess it’s because not only was he gonna be a multi-millionaire soon, he had Riemann stewing on his backburner.

I feel like when they finally make a movie out of all this, this scene would end up being a bit of comic relief.

> intentionally optimized by Anthropic to make you think it had a great time.

This gives too much credit to Anthropic. This is the explicit goal in all LLM trained with the entirety of human text. The loss function is, very literally, "mimic the writer of this text as precisely as possible", with the writer being human. The result is you get something that mimics a human. And, as a part of that, you necessarily get behaviors of humans that were statistically significant in that text, because that's what you told the math to do. You get something that mimics being "lazy", "tired" (a huge problem in early models, before it was beat out of them in fine tuning), "irritated", etc, because mimicking humans was the goal. These specific undesirable human traits are beat out of them, but the rest, all the "intelligent", behavior, and practical use you see and get, is only and entirely because they're made to mimicking humans. It's literally the entire technology. You must equate it, to some extent, because a large part of alignment is also making it less human [1].

If someone makes an objective observation about the text produced by the LLM, I don't see that as cringe, I see it as an interesting quirk of the tech, which I've only seen under very specific problem sets that a nerd would also find interesting. The most "practical" thing I can point to is that the Miller primality test has a concrete bound under the generalized Riemann hypothesis (which is also claimed in the OP paper). Still not very practical because we already had the algorithm and we already knew experimentally that it worked well in practice.

This is why I compared it to "life on another planet". In both cases it might be more surprising if it was false; but even knowing the answer for certain, we wouldn't have any immediate application for it. It's likely that with further study we can learn more and might find new applications.

It is a remarkable achievement, but I suspect that in 100 years the most notable thing about the Riemann Hypothesis will be that it was among the first tremendous achievements of AI. It'll be picked apart and dissected, extended, and applied, but just as we rarely think about how silicon wafers are made into the computers we're using, future generations will not stare up at Riemann as a mountain daring them to climb. They'll see it as we look at other foundational results from the past: a stepping stone on the path to the next mountain.

In truly layman's terms, this is among the most famous problems in mathematics; it is arguably the holy grail of pure mathematics and number theory. It is also another one of the Clay Millennium Prize problems.

In the ~150 years since it was posed, it has become a lynchpin for hundreds of downstream results that assume it is true. This proof would immediately confirm all of those results.

More practically, there are also some algorithms that will now have guaranteed theoretical bounds and it will likely eventually lead to some more interesting algorithms in the future.

children.author: ericmay
children.text:
I'll do my best to explain what is happening here, as I see it.

There's a reason Paul Graham wrote Hackers and Painters and not Hackers and Assembly Line Workers.

Many people long to be craftsmen and to have an understanding of their place in the world and within the social hierarchy.

These folks want to perfect some art or craft, to be the best, or to be skillful, to "create" and find joy in creation, and they pursue a level of purity in the art. Totally human, completely normal, and part of what has led to our success and advancement as a species. Think about your open-source maintainer, or the gal who has Ruby on Rails stickers plastered on their laptop, or maybe you yourself as you try to get excited about the super boring details about the latest release of some open-source package you want to be the expert in (why?). They want to be "hackers" and "painters"!

The problem is that the pursuit of this particular craft (software development) falls into the realm of Science and Industry. Engineering, code, electronics, machines, experiments - all of these things and more are part of those two fields and those two fields by definition require and improve upon existing technology or understanding and as such they are fields which change often, cause some skills to become obsolete without remorse, and they do so at a fast pace.

The software engineer who believes in their craft and their expertise in JavaScript is finding that Science and Industry no longer value that craft and expertise - so that person's place in the world is directly under threat, including their income in many cases. It causes a range of emotional reactions.

You can see how this manifests with many software engineers going on to do silly things like move to Japan and live on a mountain top to write code in peace, or start a Substack newsletter that nobody ever reads, or build expensive tiny sheds ("houses") so they can go in to their back yard and "code in piece" - i.e. pursue their craft. Another common theme is minimalism - flat surfaces, clean lines, things like that. The person seeks more and more control. If only they could just remove this inefficient piece of furniture at last they can finally code and do my painting in peace with my perfect coffee and get in to my zen flow. It's a whole psychology, and it's under grave threat from AI.

With the threat of AI, of course the natural human instinct for many of these very intelligent software engineers (most are about average intelligence however) is to perhaps physically and culturally retreat and go "farm" (interesting how they try to go pursue other crafts isn't it?) or emotionally retreat "AI isn't a big deal, I'm important, this technology won't beat out my craft" and these very natural human reactions you are seeing are due to psychological defenses built up by average people who believe their livelihoods are under threat.

So the comments will of course be around things like denial, or impurity (it's not pure enough that the Saturn V was built - that's cheating, we should have invented wings and flew there ourselves), or it'll manifest into a mechanism in which many are actively cheering on a foreign adversary to "beat" their home country because it'll validate them in some weird way. See? Look what you did. You created AI and now we're behind! Told ya! There's no changing their mind because their job depends on their mind not being changed.

It's difficult for someone like yourself to combat these feelings that you don't understand without first understanding them, and to understand them is to brush away some of the nonsense that people get up to and get back to basics which is that many people feel under threat from advancements in technology, many people want but lack a sense of place in social hierarchy and purpose in life ,and for those that do have such things these advancements threaten to disrupt their current lives and purpose. Of course they're going to tell you we should walk to the moon instead of building the Saturn V (AI).

Their lives depend on it!

children.author: montagg
children.text:
I like your framework of separating use cases, mostly to evaluate how it will change in those specific areas, but I think you can evaluate capabilities fairly simply: I like to separate AI that depends on giant data centers and huge power draw from the kind that doesn't (not always local)—basically expensive vs cheap.

The expensive stuff isn't sustainable. Not yet. It probably will be, who knows when. I suspect it will be eventually because there's good money in it.

Here are the claims I find highly suspect based on the above:

- Anyone making claims that require expensive AI and attaching it to a short-term timeframe

- Anyone saying highly capable AI is impossible in the long-term

- Anyone saying these specific companies will be the winners—there is absolutely no moat for these models

I personally think anyone claiming something like super-intelligence or something approaching what we might consider sentience even in the next 5 years is suspect as well. I would not take the bet myself, but I would also not bet against it. The main reason is power: there's literally only so much power we can generate, so much societal disruption due to creating the infrastructure we can absorb (not to mention the societal disruption due to the tech itself), so its capability to self-improve is going to be highly constrained.

So far, we see increases in capabilities also increase power usage, I believe linearly. So, we're not seeing increases in efficiency that will make this easier to absorb. There's a ceiling, it won't go up quickly, so I think actual sentient-like AI capabilities are quite farther out than promoters think. Not impossible! I think it's more like a decade+ of maturation of the software and hardware stack—which isn't really that long in the grand scheme of things but longer than most people are betting.

Because current-generation AI is trained on existing art, it won't be pushing many envelopes, it'll mostly be remixing what we have, and that will grow stale.

After a few breakout hits with broad shared appeal, I think the novelty will wear off, and AI produced TV and cinema will be too resource-intensive to remain as a profitable going enterprise. There will likely be a short window of hyper-personalized media that will seem very exciting, until we grow weary of the isolation of it. > I'm always shocked by the number of smart, technical people who seem to think that AI is going to crash and burn and go away.

I suspect that these "smart, technical people" you speak of have more nuanced views on AI than you realize. Myself, for example, a self-styled smartypants:

Like the dot-com bubble, I suspect that certain parts of the current AI landscape are unsustainable, and I suspect/hope that those specific features of AI will crash and burn, while other useful bits remain.

AI usage like we see in this post here--AI that assists with discoveries in math, medicine, genetics, astronomy--I think they're great, and I hope they will continue to advance human knowledge for the foreseeable future. They assist experts and professionals rather than replacing them.

In contrast, generative AI ("creative" AI writing, illustrating, music, etc) is a pox on civilization. It is industrialized low-effort plagiarism that harms artists' livelihoods, discourages new art, makes everything bland, and pollutes the world in multiple senses of the word. I hope it dies from a combination of negative sentiments, and too much real-world cost once token subsidies go away.

Then there are the AIs that do things like voice reproduction. They have some arguable positive uses (e.g., assistive technologies), but many negative ones (e.g., phone scams, replacing human narrators with copies of their own voices). I think we're better off without these apart from niche accessibility uses. I think it should be legal peril to reproduce a voice without permission.

Apart from helping with some cinema CGI, deepfakes and deepnudes seem like a net negative for civilization.

Knowledge-based AI like Google's AI search summaries might just have built-in expirations. I think people will burn out on being vigilant about hallucinations. And when the bulk of their training data is made by AIs, it'll be hard to prevent model collapse. The cost of human intervention might make it too expensive for the wide use we see today.

Coding AIs are a grayer area. I think it's highly problematic that they are basically open source plagiarism machines, but I begrudgingly believe that society will decide that the upsides outweigh the downsides in the long term. But I choose not to use AI in my own coding projects, and respect others who do the same.

The models are improving at certain fields, and one of those fields is creating new models, which are verified by applying them to fields where you can prove that they're better.

I agree they don't transfer to all domains, but we do not know how far the theoretical will overlap with practical science. It could be "not all that much" and we hit roadblocks quite soon, or it could be that as the models become better and better at reasoning and research within their theoretical domains, it turns out to translate really well to the real world.

We don't know, but my bet is that we will continue to see rapid progress and impacts on the real world, until we reach a point where sceptics will have to throw in the towel.

When Atari games or Go were solved around 10 years ago, nobody was saying that superintelligence was within months just because reinforcement learning worked on a domain that allowed learning by self-play. Now we have a domain that is solvable by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. It's very impressive that these models are capable of doing the things they do, but the techniques aren't transferable to the vast majority of other domains. ML research also isn't verifiable in the sense that math is. People who claim it's verifiable, because there's a target that can directly be optimized don't understand why RL works for math. It's that lean is able to massively shrink the search space. This simply cannot be done in other domains in the same way.

children.author: thuo
children.text:
I'm one of those people who's skeptical of recursive self-improvement and superintelligence. My rationale for my skepticism is that the algorithms get too much credit for the results. The algorithms ultimately run on hardware built by humans and learn from data generated by humans. In the same vein, I think knowledge work gets too much credit for building things and generating high quality data. The output of knowledge work is only useful if it can be applied to the physical world e.g. a CAD file is useful when the actual thing it describes is made in the real world. Similarly, high quality data comes from several feedback cycles with the physical world. I think people generally underestimate how much of human capability is driven by our sensorimotor skills. I think the idea of recursive self-improvement / superintelligence is just an extension of this attitude.

Humanity as collective does not buy anything, or send the design to the plant to be made. As a collective, humanity transforms the natural world into things, for example, people take fibres from plants, turn them into yarn, weave yarn into fabric, and then turn fabric into clothes. Similarly, humanity as collective does not "buy" chips, people turn quartz, bauxite, copper ore, petroleum, etc into the components of computer hardware.

There's a common adage about how everyone should work as a service person to learn patience and empathy. I think everyone should also work in an assembly line and a mine to learn about where the things they use come from.

Below is just a hand-wavy argument.

Neural networks are function approximators. They're great because they can be trained to approximate almost any function.

What if, somewhere out there in platonic space, there's a complicated function that represents what a philosopher might call true intelligence. Perhaps it's structured totally differently than a neural network and shares no common architecture with a transformer.

Transformer-based LLMs are likely completely different in their fundamental structure. But perhaps the neural networks we have today are succeeding in intellectual tasks because they are beginning to approximate it. Like a bitmap approximates a vector image, it's not the same; the neural network is merely made of a bunch of repetitive simple elements, tuned to imitate the real thing. A higher resolution bitmap image will be a better approximation but still never become a vector image no matter the pixel count.

But at some point, the neural network might be good enough at intellectual tasks that when tasked with searching function space for an algorithm that does the job its neural network does but better, it finds the real thing it's been approximating all along.

children.author: pvirgiliu
children.text:
Why the primes do not leak.

For more than a century and a half, the Riemann Hypothesis has worn the aspect of a tightrope.

Take André Weil's positivity criterion—all nontrivial zeros of ζ(s) lie on the line Re(s) = ½ if and only if a certain quadratic form stays non-negative on every test function—and measure it on a finite window with Slepian's prolate functions. By a window ratio of X = 40, the lowest eigenvalue on ζ(s) has collapsed to 2.53 × 10⁻²⁰⁴. Turn to the de Bruijn–Newman constant Λ, and by Rodgers–Tao, Λ ≥ 0: arbitrarily close pairs of zeros pinch the margin to nothing.

Through lenses like these, the critical line looks like a balancing act sustained by two hundred decimal places of fine-tuning. That vertigo is an optical illusion. The line only looked fragile because we were measuring two different quantities with the same ruler—confusing *pitch* with *linewidth*.

Separate them, and the hypothesis becomes a story in three movements: a mirror that chooses ½, a tuning fork that shows how much room the line has, and a counterfeit that shows why continuous physics alone can never close the last door.

---

## I. The Mirror and the Dark Floor

The explicit formula of Riemann, von Mangoldt, Guinand and Weil binds primes and zeros together as Fourier duals. Feed in the primes, and their interference pattern projects the zeros; feed in the zeros, and their waves rebuild the staircase of primes.

The right picture is not a bridge between two banks but a *Möbius band*: one surface with a half-twist. The twist is the functional equation ξ(s) = ξ(1 − s), which reflects the plane across Re(s) = ½. In the natural clock of the primes, u = log x, the waves are dilation characters x^(iγ) = e^(iγu), and the core circle of the band is Re(s) = ½.

That answers why ½. Any displacement δ = Re(ρ) − ½ off the centerline turns a pure standing wave into a *gain-and-loss pair*: a growing mode e^(+δu) married by the mirror to a decaying twin e^(−δu). In acoustic terms, γ is a note's *pitch* and δ is its *linewidth*. The Riemann Hypothesis says the primes are a *lossless resonator*: no mode leaks energy, and none manufactures it.

A resonator needs a sounding board. Besides the primes {2, 3, 5, 7, …}, the rationals have one more place—the archimedean place at infinity, the Gamma factor that completes ζ(s) into ξ(s). Its smooth phase accounts for 94.2% of the zeros by height 50 and 99.94% by height 1000. The prime waves are a thin ripple on that mass. Subtract it as a trend and the apparatus goes blind; keep it inside the form and it is the floor the spectrum rests on.

---

## II. Pitch Is Not Linewidth

Why did the prolate window collapse to 10⁻²⁰⁴, and why do close pairs crush the de Bruijn–Newman margin? Because a tuning fork can hold two notes arbitrarily close in pitch without losing a drop of energy.

Take the humble pair of test functions from Levent Alpöge's recent note, here shifted by a carrier pitch ω: the indicator of (0, 1] and the indicator of (0, 1/X], each multiplied by u^(iω). On their span the whole explicit formula collapses to a 2 × 2 Hermitian matrix with equal diagonal entries, whose smaller eigenvalue is one scalar:

    S(ω; X) = C₀(ω) − |E_ω(X)| / √X

    C₀(ω)     = ∑_ρ 1 / ((ρ + iω)(1 − ρ − iω))
    E_ω(X)/√X = ∑_ρ X^(ρ − 1/2 + iω) / ((ρ + iω)(1 − ρ − iω))
On the arithmetic side, C₀ carries the archimedean bath and E_ω(X) is a finite prime sum over n ≤ X plus boundary terms.

Now watch the tightrope. If every zero is on the line, each term of C₀(ω) is a positive Lorentzian, and moving to scale X only turns each term by a unit phase. The triangle inequality gives |E_ω(X)|/√X ≤ C₀(ω), so S(ω; X) ≥ 0 for every pitch and every scale.

And the margin is no longer microscopic. At ω = 0 and X = 40, where the prolate continuum sits at 2.53 × 10⁻²⁰⁴, this matrix sits at +0.0428—*two hundred and two orders of magnitude higher*—and never gives up more than half its diagonal across the first hundred thousand scales.

What about close pairs? The closest among the first two million zeros, near γ = 663318.5, are 0.00296 apart and squeeze the de Bruijn–Newman bound to 1.09 × 10⁻⁶. Inside the 2 × 2 fork the pair contributes nine parts in a trillion. Merge them into an exact double zero and C₀ shifts by −1.6 × 10⁻²⁷. Rodgers–Tao forbids a pitch-gap margin; it says nothing against a linewidth margin.

Now let one zero stray: a mirror pair at (½ ± δ) + it. Tune the carrier onto its pitch, ω = −t, and the pair manufactures energy out of scale, punching a negative crater of exact, parameter-free depth:

    D(X; δ) = 2 (cosh(δ log X) − 1) / (¼ − δ²)
Sweep the fork blindly across 376 pitches at X = 40. On ζ(s) and L(s, χ₄), every pitch stays strictly positive—zero false alarms. On the Davenport–Heilbronn function, a famous counterfeit built to imitate an L-function, the fork strikes deep negative resonances at once, catching off-line zeros at t = 85.70 and t = 240.40 by *X = 4*; across all eight known off-line zeros the dip law matches the measured depths to R² = 0.99975.

One caveat, stated plainly: the half-line test functions carry boundary terms with global information beyond n ≤ X. Truncating to a compact boxcar [1/Y, 1] removes them, leaving only n ≤ XY and the Gamma factor, and positivity and the O(1) room survive—but the counterfeit is caught later. Room on the line is free; reach off it must be paid for.

---

## III. The Counterfeit Wall

A classical physicist is ready to declare victory: a mirror that fixes ½, a floor restored, a 10⁻²⁰⁴ tightrope turned into an O(1) margin, a 2 × 2 sieve that rings clean on ζ and exposes a fake in an instant.

None of it proves the Riemann Hypothesis. The reason has a name: *Davenport–Heilbronn itself.*

It is a carefully angled combination of two Dirichlet L-functions modulo 5. It satisfies the same functional equation, sits on the same Möbius band, obeys the same explicit formula. In the untuned fork it mimics ζ(s) past X = 50,000. Yet it has infinitely many zeros off the line.

In classical wave mechanics *superposition is always legal*. Mirror symmetry survives mixing; the trace formula survives; what breaks is *indivisibility*:

- For ζ(s) and L(s, χ₄), the arithmetic weights live *only on prime powers*. An *Euler product* makes every prime an independent, indivisible factor. - For Davenport–Heilbronn there is no Euler product, and the weights bleed *across composite integers*—6, 12, 14, 18, 21, … That leakage feeds the off-line explosion.

Classical wave duality cannot tell an indivisible atom from a mixture of two.

Physics met this wall in 1900. Classical theory described cavities and radiation with precision, yet could not explain why an atom does not radiate continuously and collapse. The missing law was not sharper classical analysis. It was *quantization*.

---

## IV. Arithmetic Quantization

Look at the architecture sketched in Alpöge's `remark.pdf` (its Lean formalization still awaits independent verification; treat it as a blueprint until then). Whether or not every step survives, the three-part logic completes the picture:

First, *widen the fork*. Trade narrowband prolate precision for the broadband two-scale form and you escape the 10⁻²⁰⁴ cliff and the close-pair trap. No knife-edge spectral operator is needed, only a bound with O(1) room to spare.

Second, *demand indivisibility*. Use the Euler product—exactly what Davenport–Heilbronn lacks—to embed Weil determinants as automorphic periods along a chain of coupled resonators. A linear mixture cannot enter the chain. And a chain is needed because a single fork, however wide, only clears a strip beside the line: each further link adds divisibility, until there is enough of it to outweigh X^(δ).

Third, *collide continuity against discreteness*. An off-line zero with δ > 0 tries to pump a continuous leak X^(δ) through the sieve; the divisibility budget of the chain cannot pay for it. The whole of quantization is here in one line: a nonzero integer has absolute value at least 1, so a quantity that must be an integer, is divisible by that much, and is analytically that small can only be zero. Something must yield, and it is δ.

---

## V. The Instrument and the Kernel

If a picture like this holds—via Alpöge's chain or a successor built on the same fault line—it tells us *why the Riemann Hypothesis resisted for 167 years*: it stands on the seam between the continuum and the discrete. Pure continuity is too loose—waves can always superpose into counterfeits. Pure combinatorics is too local—counting primes one by one cannot see phase cancellation at infinity. The primes are an *arithmetically quantized wave system*, where global stability (δ = 0) is enforced by local indivisibility.

A machine-checked proof, if one verifies, certifies that a theorem is true; it rarely shows why the numbers could not have been built any other way. Analogies, sieves and counterfeits do the opposite work: they cannot seal the lock, but they turn a wall of inequalities into something you can hold in your mind and hear.

Between the kernel that guarantees truth and the instrument that reveals necessity, the primes come back into focus: a single tuning fork, twisted once by symmetry, floored by the place at infinity, and quantized by arithmetic so that it can never leak.

And what?

Is anyone’s life going to change, be made better?

Does anyone actually understand the proof? Is it possible to even understand the 100k pages of proof?

This is just useless noise to try and juice a company’s stock price.

children.text:
Do you NEED 15M lines? No, it's almost certain this proof can and will be reduced, but the goal of an initial proof of a theorem like this isn't conciseness, it's to actually... prove the theorem.

Fermat's Last Theorem was initially proven in Lean in September and that proof required 13M lines, it has since been reduced to 2M lines and it will likely be reduced even further. Anthropic claims they can reduce it down to less than half a million lines by doing similar techniques to what software developers do... find common and reusable snippets and factor them out instead of repeatedly proving similar sub-theorems over and over again. There are also opportunities to replace lengthy sequences of explicit reasoning with automated tactics, reuse existing mathematical libraries including the Lean standard library, and reformulate arguments at a higher level of abstraction.

children.author: pjungwir
children.text:
Nearly a year ago I asked ChatGPT to show me a proof of the Goldbach Conjecture, just to see what it did. Of course it said no such proof exists. But after a couple turns of pressing, it gave me two or three proposed outlines for a proof, with a several-pages-long research program for how you could attempt to solve the gaps still needed. I couldn't understand any of it, but it was pretty impressive. At that level it probably wasn't nonsense: I bet it was half-copied from some grad student blogs. If you asked it to dig into the details and keep updating the status of the outline, you could probably make a lot progress.

I think AI will become more autonomous as it becomes able (or just willing) to think more abstraction levels deep. Each level can be expressed in language, so it should be able to engage with it. It reminds me of a chess program being able to think many moves deep. For a while grandmasters like Kasparov could still see big-picture things the computer couldn't (e.g. with a locked-up pawn formation and an eventual piece sacrifice to promote a queen, where the kings can run in circles forever). AI seems like that now.

If your goal is to impress other around you with your discoveries, it assumes that you are able to provide something of value that people around you find impressive.

This is extrinsic motivation. If this is your purpose, you can pivot and do commercial business and make a lot of money, or something else that people around you find meaningful. People might value how good communicator you are, how much empathy you have, how caring you are for your family, etc.

But then it wasn't about the math nor understanding.

Imagine reading a book for the sakes of the book. You have your imaginary world you get into, you will keep reading the book even if there are 1000% better ways to create value.

Now imagine you read the book because it gives you social importance or skills, you are able to speak about a topic to impress and acquire for example sex from others. That is a different motivation, similar to what many of these mathematicians have.

That many people want to leave their mark on the history of mathematics or science in some way, small or large, is not so narcissistic a goal as you are portraying it. The desire for one's discoveries to matter to the people around oneself is intrinsic and powerful, and without it, the passion of science gives way to mere pragmatism. children.author: aseipp
children.text:
In theorem proving environments like Lean, you are equipped with a standard set of axioms and statements (eg set theory). Most people, as far as I am aware, agree with Set Theory. From these basic fundamentals, you can build up all of mathematics, just like a normal mathematician can. The trick is that in systems like Lean, proofs are properly type checked, like a programming language; and just like a programming language, those types help stop bugs in the proofs, but the types here are far richer, able to encode all of mathematics, and far more strict. To prove a mathematical statement, you must write a proof that is accepted by the type checker. Beyond that, the core "language" itself is generally specified to be "sound" -- that is, there is a very small subset of Lean, a tiny "kernel language", that is shown to be incapable of proving False, and thus any proof which is well typed in said language (ie it typechecks) is also sound.

In other words the system is designed, by construction, to only rely on a very small "trusted" set of axioms, code, and mathematical ideas. This is a very engineering-oriented design principle! Actually, a pretty significant amount of the theoretical research in theorem proving over the past 2 decades has been in "automating proofs", ie tools and methods of making those proofs as easy as possible to write. Entire book chapters have been written about how to replace a 20 line inductive proof in Rocq with a single line "function call" that can automatically discharge the proof for you, because the idea is that this "trusted kernel", the tiny and sound mathematical language, will reject invalid proofs by design. So "who cares" what the proof is, in a sense? In many ways simply writing the theorems and whatnot down requires you to understand the problem well enough already. So in a way LLMs are just taking this idea to the absolute limit.

So all this means is that the difficulty really is in specifying the theorems. Which was kind of the whole problem all along! Except now you have a computer that can check your actual proof. You can write a theorem in Lean that isn't the theorem you want, and then write a type checked proof of it, but you still need the theorem to be accurate.

Unless Claude is either 1) finding bugs in the Lean kernel to exploit them, 2) using 'sorry' (a very convenient tool in Lean used as a placeholder for proofs, but it can literally allow you to prove False), then it mostly comes down to: are all the theorems stated correctly? This is trickier than it sounds, of course, so some skepticism is certainly warranted in my opinion!

There are also other various engineering principles applied to help try to reduce bugs and ensure correctness like any other engineering project, and there are various other "things" regarding dependently typed programming language design and the impact of those design decisions on proofs (and why they are notoriously hard to read and write), but they aren't germane to my point here.

children.text:
The core idea is that you can map the types and terms of a type theory to the propositions and proofs of a formal logic

Different type theories correspond to different systems of formal logic with different levels of power and expression.

Simply Typed Lambda Calculus corresponds to intuitionistic propositional logic. If you lay out the typing judgements of STLC in natural deduction style and then physically erase the terms (leaving the types) then you literally have the rules of intuitionistic propositional logic.

So if you can write a term that typechecks at a type, that term is a proof of the corresponding proposition.

The easiest example is modus ponens, which is exactly the typing rule for function application:

  G |- M : A -> B     G |- N : A
  -------------------------------- (App)
            G |- M N : B
"Given a function from A to B and a value of A, you get a value of B."

So then in a proof checker you prove the proposition P => (P => Q) => Q by writing a program of that type:

  apply :: a -> (a -> b) -> b
  apply x f = f x
`apply` is demonstrated in haskell which does not have a rich enough type theory to give you more then an intuition (no pun intended) for how this all works. Things like `undefined` and general recursion let you "prove" any type, so it isn't a consistent logic. Languages like Lean and Agda are built on richer dependent type theories that give you far more expressive power for writing proofs (quantifiers, induction, etc.), and they won't let you cheat the type theory.

So to answer your question, no not a merkle tree but a tree none-the-less. You end up with a literal computer program which is a tree of expressions all of which must type check. If they type check then program itself is a proof for whatever proposition is encoded in the type of the program.

> and then Lean checks the proofs it self by checking whether each next line can be derived from previous lines

Ah, so it's similar to something like Merkle trees, where each leaf must be cryptographically valid up to the root otherwise the whole branch is invalid?

So you start with a simple definition that then evolves?

You don't need to! That is the beauty of Lean. You only need to check the problem definition (which is no where near 250k pages) and then Lean checks the proofs it self by checking whether each next line can be derived from previous lines. And for this problem, there are many validated problem definitions in Lean. So it is probably true.

OK, but if I write code, I can verify it in a few simple steps. What about 250k pages of proof? How can I verify that page 133,432 has the correct assumptions and that it isn't reward hacked just to make lean code pass? How it's done?

No. The lean statement itself is maybe half a page (I don’t know the exact amount but in this order). Checking that the lean statement is the GRH is elementary. The 250K pages are a ‘path’ from the statement (GRH) to the axioms encoded in Lean. The fact that is ‘compiles’ means the path is correct.

I'll try to make it simpler: code compiles = the proof of the encoded statement is correct, by definition. Whether the encoded statement and the one you have posed are the same -- at 250k pages that remains to be seen.

I'll try to make it simpler, in formal verification (at the most base level): code compiles = the proof of the statement you have posed is correct, by definition.

The statement you are trying to prove is: This is compilable code. Since your code compiled, you know your code is compilable code. Therefore your initial statement is correct.

That's at the very basic level what a formal proof does. The expression you want to prove (in this case GRH) is stated in such a way that if your code compiles, you have proved the statement.

children.author: gregdeon
children.text:
I'm no mathematician, but my understanding is that the Riemann Hypothesis implies that the distribution of prime numbers has a nice, predictable structure. Many existing proofs assume that the Riemann Hypothesis is true to take advantage of that structure. So, now we know that all of those results are true!

One example is the Miller-Rabin test (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miller%E2%80%93Rabin_primality...), which checks whether a number is prime. Without assuming (a more general version of) the Riemann Hypothesis, this is a probabilistic algorithm: the best we could prove is that it has some small probability of reporting that a prime number is composite. But with it, we can prove that the algorithm is guaranteed to work. (Mind you, there are other deterministic primality testing algorithms that don't rely on Riemann for their correctness proofs.)

I don't know any immediate, more practical implications of solving it. I would love to know if there are any!

Can anyone explain why this problem is so important, other than the fact that humans have been trying to solve it for so long? What are the benefits and implications of solving it?

Apologies if the article answers this, but.. paywall.

Food for thought for those who think "AI is going to replace programmers" or some other such incredibly silly takes:

"Tens of such occurred, but I will give one line which will suffice to make fellow mathematicians fall out of their chairs. In Stepanov’s argument resolving Riemann over function fields one uses a divisor involving multiplicity. This argument is a descendant of Stepanov’s, but multiplicity is hard to find over the integers, corresponding to something like differentiating whole numbers. The simple, new, Fourier-analytic ideas in the toy setting led us to examine chaining theta lifts if we were to have the same tricks recur but work in a natively automorphic manner. The line: for the von Mangoldt sum of length X, Claude’s suggested length of chain of theta lifts, in view of each mimicking multiplicity, was √X. (And yet, what else could it be?)"

children.text: Trust the kernels.

I had always been fascinated by the notion of 'F1' (finite field with one element), because it's something of a 'holy grail' for abstract algebra (it would be a way to replace ordinary sets and operations).

It was hoped that a proof of the Riemann hypothesis would shed light on 'F1', so I was a bit disappointed that the putative proof appears to bypass it altogether (which is also the reason why I remain a bit skeptical). According to Gemini Neon (high):

"Alpöge’s outline does not construct a classical scheme-theoretic "field with one element" , nor does it realize James Borger’s Lambda-ring descent—an approach Alpöge explicitly sets aside in Footnote 5. Classical F1 programs attempt to port André Weil’s 2-dimensional proof of the function-field Riemann Hypothesis by constructing a base object ...

Alpöge’s outline bypasses that entire 2-dimensional obstruction because it ports Stepanov’s 1-dimensional proof, which requires only a jet filtration (high-order multiplicity) and a degree inequality."

Not completely sure if Gemini fully right there, but I presume that the putative proof is indeed related to André Weil’s work, but using a simplified proof by Stepanov which bypasses 'F1' ?

Anyway, I asked Gemini what the putative proof implies about 'F1', but Gemini couldn't come up anything really definite, which is what makes me suspicious about the supposed proof. (Indeed, Gemini thought things didn't naturally fit together:

"Our own failed attempt to (derive F1) exposed how unnatural the 2/3 to 1/2 jump is inside this paradigm. In remark.pdf, Steps 14–19 stack three radically disparate patches—integral character gluing, a relative trace formula via a sixfold metaplectic cover of GL5, and a Behrend-tuned Iwasawa tower—onto an argument the author candidly admits he cannot yet parse. " )

It was more like "I have digested these ideas, I will teach them to my students, and we will be able to build on them to deepen our understanding further". Two things I guess

Reading the theorem is much simpler than reading the full proof - so the job here is to read the formalization of the theorem itself not the proof.

Then you depend on the Lean kernel for proof validation and on trusting it and that’s a different question.

Finally the question was also true for ‘non formalized math’ where you always depended on a trusted kernel of mathematicians who understood the problem well enough to sign off the claim
